summary: The page resolves the Yoma/Middot contradiction about the Chamber of the Lambs by identifying Middot's author. Rav Huna attributes Middot to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, supported by a mishna in which he admits that he forgot the function of the southwest chamber of the Women's Courtyard. The Gemara then tests the attribution through the measurements of the eastern approach: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's extra step and platform explain why the Sanctuary entrance was hidden, but Rav Adda bar Ahava argues that Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar provides an alternative explanation.

display.title: Identify the author, not the winner: resolving the Yoma/Middot contradiction
display.whats: Rav Huna resolves a contradiction about chamber placement by identifying who authored Tractate Middot: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov. This is proved by a mishna where he admits he forgot the function of the southwest chamber of the Women's Courtyard; Abba Shaul identifies it as the House of Oils.
display.hint: How does Rav Huna identify R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as Middot's author, and how does the forgotten function of the southwest chamber prove it?

learning.learnerQuestion: If a Mishnah's chamber placements conflict with another source, how can we know which tannaitic view it reflects?
learning.coreTension: A Mishnah's chamber list needs to be matched to a known tanna before its placements can be understood as that tanna's view.
learning.coreMove: Rav Huna does not pick a winner between the two texts. He identifies who wrote Middot - R. Eliezer ben Yaakov - using a second Middot mishna where he admits that he forgot the function of the southwest chamber of the Women's Courtyard, which Abba Shaul identifies as the House of Oils.
learning.resolution: Rav Huna identifies R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as the author of Middot, so its chamber placements reflect his tradition, while a conflicting source reflects another tannaitic view.

takeaway.text: An apparent contradiction between authoritative texts can be resolved by identifying the tannaitic view represented by one of them rather than assuming that a source made an error.

learning.ahaMoment: The architectural contradiction is resolved by identifying Middot's author: its chamber placement reflects R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's tradition.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat the disagreement between Yoma and Middot as a textual error rather than recognizing that Rav Huna resolves it by identifying the tannaitic view represented by Middot.
learning.memoryAnchor: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov authored Middot - proven by his admission that he forgot the function of the southwest chamber, which Abba Shaul identifies as the House of Oils.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Huna: Middot authored by R. Eliezer ben Yaakov
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Huna
argumentFlow.text: Tractate Middot was authored by R. Eliezer ben Yaakov; therefore the chamber placements in Middot's own mishnah reflect his individual view.

argumentFlow.label: Proof: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov admits forgetting in Middot
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The mishna in Middot records R. Eliezer ben Yaakov admitting that he forgot what the southwest chamber of the Women's Courtyard was used for, while the other three chambers' purposes are stated without any such admission.

sourceRefs.note: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's admission of forgetting

argumentFlow.label: Therefore Middot's chamber placement is R. EbY's view
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Since R. Eliezer ben Yaakov authored Middot, the chamber placements in Middot's mishnah reflect his position, resolving the contradiction with the other source.

sourceRefs.note: Middot's author is R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, confirmed by his own admission of forgetting

misconceptions.misconception: Rav Huna is merely naming a Mishnah's author rather than using that identification to validate its chamber placements.
misconceptions.correction: Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by identifying R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as Middot's author, so Middot's placement reflects his tannaitic view.

quizSeeds.answer: He identifies R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as the author of Middot, establishing that Middot's chamber placements reflect his tannaitic view.

quizSeeds.answer: A second Middot mishna in which R. Eliezer ben Yaakov admits that he forgot the function of the southwest chamber of the Women's Courtyard; Abba Shaul identifies it as the House of Oils.

sugyot.finalRuling: Rav Huna identifies R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as the author of Tractate Middot, so the chamber placements in Middot's mishnah reflect his tannaitic view, resolving the contradiction.

display.title: Testing Middot's authorship through the eastern approach
display.whats: The Gemara totals the elevations from the eastern gate toward the Sanctuary: the soreg and cheil, the stairway rising from the Women's Courtyard into the Israelites' Courtyard, the stairway between the Entrance Hall and the altar, and R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's extra step and platform. This initially explains why the Sanctuary entrance was hidden from the priest on the Mount of Olives, but Rav Adda bar Ahava argues that Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar could provide an alternative explanation.
display.hint: Which two explanations are offered for why the lower Sanctuary entrance was hidden: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's added elevation or Rabbi Yehuda's centered altar?

learning.learnerQuestion: Do the Temple's eastern elevations independently prove that Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov?
learning.coreTension: The lower Sanctuary entrance was hidden from the priest on the Mount of Olives, and the Gemara tests which tannaitic Temple plan explains that obstruction.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara adds the soreg and cheil, the stairways, and R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's extra step and platform. His added elevation initially explains why the entrance was hidden, but Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges the attribution by invoking Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar as an alternative obstruction.
learning.resolution: The measurements first support R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's plan, because his extra step and platform hide the entrance. Rav Adda bar Ahava rejects this as decisive proof and argues that Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar also blocks the lower entrance.

takeaway.text: A measurement-based attribution is not decisive when another tannaitic plan can explain the same architectural observation.

learning.ahaMoment: The added elevation explains the hidden entrance, while Rav Adda bar Ahava introduces Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar as an alternative before this amud ends.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to stop at the initial measurement match and miss Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative explanation from Rabbi Yehuda.
learning.memoryAnchor: Extra step and platform: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov; centered thirty-two-cubit altar: Rabbi Yehuda.

argumentFlow.label: Test Middot through the eastern elevations
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara tests whether the measurements of the Temple's eastern approach fit R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's plan.

argumentFlow.label: Soreg and cheil establish the first rise
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The calculation begins with the soreg and the ten-cubit cheil on the eastern approach.

argumentFlow.label: Count the three stairway sets toward the Sanctuary
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara counts twelve steps rising through the rampart into the Women's Courtyard, fifteen steps rising from there into the Israelites' Courtyard, and twelve steps between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

argumentFlow.label: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov adds a step and platform
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov adds another step and a platform above the standard stairways, increasing the elevation of the approach.

argumentFlow.label: The added elevation hides the entrance
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: With R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's added elevation, the lower Sanctuary entrance is hidden from the priest standing on the Mount of Olives.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges the proof
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Adda bar Ahava
argumentFlow.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava rejects the claim that the hidden entrance decisively identifies R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's plan.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Yehuda's centered altar offers an alternative
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Adda bar Ahava
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the altar stood centered in the courtyard and measured thirty-two cubits; the statement gives that measurement without explaining its consequence.

misconceptions.misconception: The elevation calculation conclusively proves that Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov.
misconceptions.correction: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges that proof by showing how Rabbi Yehuda's centered, thirty-two-cubit altar can also hide the lower entrance.

visualizableElements.item: Elevation profile from the eastern gate through the Women's and Israelites' courtyards to the Sanctuary entrance
Two obstruction models: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's added elevation and Rabbi Yehuda's centered altar

quizSeeds.question: Why do R. Eliezer ben Yaakov's extra step and platform matter to the eastern-wall argument?
quizSeeds.answer: They raise the approach enough that the lower Sanctuary entrance is hidden from the priest standing on the Mount of Olives.

quizSeeds.question: Whose view does Rav Adda bar Ahava offer as an alternative, and what feature explains the obstruction?
quizSeeds.answer: Rabbi Yehuda's view: the altar stands centered in the courtyard, directly aligned with the entrances, which is offered as an alternative explanation for why the lower entrance would be hidden; the altar is said to measure thirty-two cubits, with further detail about its shape not yet given.

sugyot.finalRuling: The elevation calculation initially supports R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, but Rav Adda bar Ahava disputes its decisiveness by offering Rabbi Yehuda's centered altar as an alternative explanation for the hidden entrance.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Which had been profaned by the kings of the idolatrous nations' - since they had burned incense on it for idol worship
in the Temple; this is taught regarding the chamber of the lambs, which is in the southwest. 'Who
taught Middot' - this is the mishna of tractate Middot itself. 'It is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's
view' - since the unattributed mishna of Middot follows his opinion. 'It was in length' - from
east to west, and in width from north
to south. 'And they send the hair under the pot' -
as it is written (Numbers 6): 'and he shall put it on the fire that is
under the peace-offering sacrifice.' 'The chamber of the metzora'im' -
explained in the next chapter, that there the metzora'im
immerse on the eighth day of their purification, when they come
to insert their hands for the thumbs, even though he had immersed
the evening before. 'Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said, I have forgotten
etc.' - it follows that the first clause is also Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's
own statement. 'So too it stands to reason' - for the unattributed
mishna of Middot is Rabbi Eliezer's own statement. 'As we learned: all
the walls, etc.' - and you cannot establish it
except as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view. 'All the walls
that were there' - throughout all the structures of the Temple Mount, they were
very much higher, so much so that all
the doorways among them were twenty cubits high, aside from
whatever was above the doorways, a great deal more
'Except the eastern wall' - it is the lower one,
at the foot of the Temple Mount, through which one enters the rampart (cheil)
before the Women's Courtyard, and from the rampart one enters
the Women's Courtyard, and from the Women's Courtyard to the
great Courtyard. 'That the priest who burns the heifer
stands on the Mount of Anointing' - that is the Mount of Olives,
which lies opposite Jerusalem to the east, with the face of
the priest turned westward. 'And he directs his gaze and sees' - from above
the height of the top of the wall, through the gateways
within it, the entrance of the Sanctuary, when he
sprinkles the blood, as it is written (Numbers 19), 'and he shall sprinkle
toward the front of the Tent of Meeting,' etc. And if
the wall were too high - even though the gateways
were aligned one opposite the other: the gate of the Temple Mount
opposite the gate of the Women's Courtyard, and the gate of the Women's
Courtyard opposite the gate of the great Courtyard,
and the gate of the Courtyard opposite the entrance of the Sanctuary - he would not
be able to see the entrance of the Sanctuary
through the gateways, since the mount continually rises
higher, until the floor level of the Sanctuary's entrance
is twenty cubits higher than the ground level at the foot of
the Temple Mount, so that the threshold of the Sanctuary turns out
to be higher than the lintel of the Temple Mount's gateway, and he could not
see the open space of the Sanctuary's entrance through

that gateway. 'And we learned: all the doorways, etc.; and we learned: within it, etc.' - all these citations of 'we learned' brought here come to explain that one never finds the lower entrance obscured
by the ascent of the Temple Mount, except according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. 'Twenty cubits high' - since they were twenty cubits high, one never finds it blocked by the ascent

of the mount, according to the Rabbis. 'Within it, a lattice-fence (soreg)' - it stood there within the eastern wall, and it was a partition made with holes like the rungs of a rope bed, and they made
it of long and short wooden boards called 'latz,' mounted one over another diagonally, called in the vernacular 'prodne.' 'Within' - from that lattice-fence

there was an open space of ten cubits, called the rampart (cheil). 'And there were twelve steps' - within that ten cubits, by which the mount rises from the lattice-fence up to the gate of the Women's Courtyard,

each step being half a cubit high, so that the floor of the Women's Courtyard rose six cubits. 'And its tread' - the width of the step's tread was half a cubit, and its length spanned the whole width of the mount,

north to south. 'Fifteen steps' - the height of the floor of the Courtyard of Israel above the Women's Courtyard, so the mount rose thirteen and a half cubits. 'And we learned: between the Entrance Hall and the altar, twelve

steps' - so the floor of the Sanctuary was higher than the floor of the lower Temple Mount by nineteen and a half cubits; there still remained, of the lower entrance, an upper half-cubit, to allow one to see

through there the lower half-cubit of the open space of the Sanctuary's entrance. 'And we learned: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says there was a step' - an additional one in the Courtyard of Israel, one cubit high, and its length spanned the width

of the whole Courtyard. 'And a platform' - of the Levites was built upon it, a cubit and a half high. 'And on it were three steps of half a cubit each' - by which they went up to the platform. 'Granted, you might say' - the unattributed teaching

that the eastern wall was low, so as to see over it through the gates of the Women's Courtyard and the Courtyard of Israel the open space of the Sanctuary's entrance. 'Is Rabbi Eliezer's view' - since he holds there was an extra step, and the floor

of the Sanctuary rose above the lower floor by twenty and a half cubits. 'That explains why it was obscured to him' - the lower entrance, at the height of the Sanctuary's floor. 'But if you say the Rabbis' hold this - the steps did not rise

except nineteen and a half cubits, and there would remain to him half a cubit by which the Sanctuary's entrance would appear visible within, to the priest standing on the Mount of Olives. 'Rav Adda bar Ahavah said: whose view is this' -

that teaches the eastern wall had to be low - it is Rabbi Yehuda's view, who says the altar stood in the middle of the Courtyard, opposite the entrances, so that its height blocked the lower entrance,
since the floor of the Courtyard of Israel rose thirteen and a half cubits above the lower floor before reaching the altar, and the altar's own height was nine - that makes twenty-two and a half
'Ten' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (explaining the ten cubits opposite the Sanctuary's entrance) continues on 16b.
